text: The case concerns the respondent State's alleged failure to protect the applicants, all of whom are members of the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex (LGBTI) community, from homophobic acts of violence by private individuals.
The case concerns the respondent State's alleged failure to conduct an effective investigation into incidents of homophobic acts of violence against the applicants.
Some applicants complained that they had been apprehended and detained unlawfully during peaceful demonstrations in support of LGBTI people.
The names of the applicants' representatives are listed in the appendix to the judgment.
The Government were initially represented by Mr M. Galperin, Representative of the Russian Federation to the European Court of Human Rights.
The Government were later represented by Mr M. Vinogradov, successor to Mr M. Galperin as Representative of the Russian Federation to the European Court of Human Rights.
The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows.
On 17 May 2012 Mr Romanov took part in the 'Rainbow flash mob' event in St Petersburg.
The 'Rainbow flash mob' event in St Petersburg on 17 May 2012 had been authorised by the local authorities.
The 'Rainbow flash mob' event in St Petersburg on 17 May 2012 marked the International Day Against Homophobia and Transphobia.
A group of people protesting against the 'Rainbow flash mob' event gathered nearby during the event on 17 May 2012.
The police were deployed to maintain public order during the 'Rainbow flash mob' event on 17 May 2012.
The police did not intervene when counter-demonstrators started insulting the participants in the 'Rainbow flash mob' event on 17 May 2012.
The parties submitted no further information about any preliminary measures which had been put in place to protect the demonstrators at the 'Rainbow flash mob' event on 17 May 2012.
During the 'Rainbow flash mob' event on 17 May 2012, Mr Romanov was holding a balloon with the inscription 'Jesus Christ loves men and women equally'.
During the 'Rainbow flash mob' event on 17 May 2012, one of the counter-demonstrators, Mr L., fired five times towards Mr Romanov with a spray gun.
While firing at Mr Romanov, Mr L. shouted 'sodomy is a mortal sin'.
As a result of Mr L.'s attack, Mr Romanov suffered chemical burns to the conjunctivae and cornea.
As a result of Mr L.'s attack, Mr Romanov suffered a contusion in the area of the right cheekbone.
The police apprehended Mr L. after the attack on Mr Romanov on 17 May 2012.
Mr L. was charged with hooliganism under Article 213 § 1 (a) of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.
In his statement of 17 May 2012, Mr L. explained that he had come to the 'Rainbow flash mob' event to 'fight sexual minorities'.
On 17 February 2013 an investigator questioned Mr L.
According to the record of the interview of 17 February 2013, Mr L. was the founder of the 'Sin-free City' movement.
One of the aims of the 'Sin-free City' movement was to fight the 'propaganda of perversion', including homosexuality.
On 17 July 2013 Mr Romanov requested the investigator to explore alleged motives of hate against LGBTI people in the case concerning the attack on him on 17 May 2012.
By a decision of 18 July 2012, the investigator dismissed Mr Romanov's request to explore hate motives against LGBTI people for 'lack of any evidence of hate motives'.

In the decision of 18 July 2012, the investigator indicated that Mr L. had not insulted anyone, had come to the event by accident, and that his actions had been motivated by the blasphemous words on the balloon.
On 11 November 2013 the Petrogradskiy District Court of St Petersburg convicted Mr L. of hooliganism under Article 213 § 1 (a) of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation as charged.
The Petrogradskiy District Court of St Petersburg sentenced Mr L. to one year's imprisonment, conditional on one year's probation.
On 18 December 2013 the State Duma of the Russian Federation amnestied Mr L.
On 12 February 2014 the St Petersburg City Court quashed the Petrogradskiy District Court's decision convicting Mr L.
On 12 February 2014 the St Petersburg City Court discontinued the case against Mr L. in accordance with the Amnesty Act.

text: On 3 November 2013 Mr Chechetkin attended the 'Rainbow Tea Social', a weekly event held to support LGBTI people, at an HIV prevention centre in St Petersburg.

At around 7.15 p.m. on 3 November 2013 two young men in hoods armed with a baseball bat and an air gun entered the HIV prevention centre in St Petersburg where the 'Rainbow Tea Social' event was being held.
The two intruders were stopped in the corridor of the HIV prevention centre by Ms P., one of the organisers of the 'Rainbow Tea Social' event.
Mr Chechetkin was nearby when the two intruders were stopped in the corridor of the HIV prevention centre on 3 November 2013.
As soon as Mr Chechetkin turned his head in the direction of the intruders, one of them shot him in the left eye with an air gun.
After being shot in the left eye, Mr Chechetkin crouched down and tried to hide.
One of the attackers shouted 'where are you going, faggot?' at Mr Chechetkin and then approached him and hit him in the shoulder and leg with a baseball bat.
After attacking Mr Chechetkin, the two men left the HIV prevention centre.
The police arrived shortly after the attack on Mr Chechetkin on 3 November 2013.
An ambulance arrived shortly after the attack on Mr Chechetkin on 3 November 2013.
The police found and collected evidence at the HIV prevention centre following the attack on 3 November 2013, including three metal bullets, several shoe prints, palm prints and fingerprints.
After the attack on 3 November 2013, Mr Chechetkin underwent surgery on his eye.
The pellet was removed from Mr Chechetkin's eye following surgery, but he lost sight in his left eye.
On 4 November 2013, at the request of Ms P., the police opened a criminal case in respect of the attack on Mr Chechetkin at the HIV prevention centre.
The attack on Mr Chechetkin on 3 November 2013 was classified under Article 213 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation as a disorderly act committed by a group.
Between November 2013 and February 2014 the police questioned Mr Chechetkin, Ms P. and more than fifteen other participants in the 'Rainbow Tea Social' event about the attack of 3 November 2013.
All persons questioned by the police between November 2013 and February 2014 about the attack of 3 November 2013 alleged that the attack had been motivated by hatred against LGBTI people.

Ms P. noted that on the day of the attack on 3 November 2013 a social network community called 'Wolf-Homophobe' ('Волк-Гомофоб') had published a post about the upcoming attack in St Petersburg on its webpage.
The investigator in the case of the attack on Mr Chechetkin identified and questioned several people who had participated in actions against the LGBTI community.
None of the fingerprints of the people questioned by the investigator in the case of the attack on Mr Chechetkin matched those found at the scene of the attack on 3 November 2013.

On 24 December 2013 the investigator refused an application by Mr Chechetkin's lawyer for the perpetrators' actions to be classified under Article 111 § 3 (a) and (b) of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation as actions committed by a group of persons for motives of hatred or enmity towards LGBTI people.

On 5 March 2014 the Leninskiy District Court of St Petersburg dismissed an appeal against the investigator's decision of 24 December 2013 refusing to classify the perpetrators' actions as motivated by hatred or enmity towards LGBTI people, holding that it was premature to decide on the legal classification of the offence at such an early stage of the proceedings.

On 21 April 2014 the St Petersburg City Court upheld the Leninskiy District Court of St Petersburg's decision of 5 March 2014 dismissing the appeal against the investigator's refusal to reclassify the offence.
On 16 July 2014 the investigator suspended the investigation into the attack on Mr Chechetkin on the grounds that the attackers could not be identified.
On 6 March 2015 the Leninskiy District Court of St Petersburg dismissed an appeal by Mr Chechetkin against the investigator's decision of 16 July 2014 to suspend the investigation.
On 6 March 2015 the Leninskiy District Court of St Petersburg dismissed a further application by Mr Chechetkin to have the perpetrators' actions classified as motivated by hatred.
On 7 May 2015 the St Petersburg City Court upheld the Leninskiy District Court of St Petersburg's decision of 6 March 2015.
The investigators suspended and resumed the investigation into the attack on Mr Chechetkin multiple times, most recently on 7 October 2017, without achieving any tangible results.
Mr Chechetkin has not received any further information about the progress of the investigation into the attack on him since 7 October 2017.

text: Article 63 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides a list of aggravated circumstances of a crime, which includes committing a crime on the grounds of political, ideological, racial, national, or religious hatred, or on the grounds of hostility or hatred towards any social group.
section_path: I. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 111 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the intentional infliction of severe harm to a person's health, the endangering of their life, or the causing of harm resulting in the loss of sight, speech, hearing or any organ or the loss of its functions, termination of a pregnancy, mental disorder, drug addiction or substance abuse, or harm resulting in the irreparable disfigurement of the face or causing a significant and persistent loss of general working capacity by at least one third or a complete loss of professional working capacity, shall be punishable by imprisonment for a term of up to eight years.
section_path: I. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 111 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the same acts as in Article 111 § 1, if committed against a person or their close relatives in connection with the performance of official duties, against a minor or person in a helpless state, in a generally dangerous manner, for hire, for disorderly motives, on the grounds of political, ideological, racial, national or religious hatred or enmity or on the grounds of hostility or hatred towards any social group, or for the purpose of using the organs or tissues of the victim, shall be punishable by imprisonment for a term of up to ten years, with or without a restriction of liberty for a term of up to two years.
section_path: I. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 111 § 3 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the acts provided for in the first or second part of Article 111, if committed by a group of persons, a group of persons upon prior conspiracy or an organised group, or against two or more persons, shall be punishable by imprisonment for a term of up to twelve years, with or without a restriction of liberty for a term of up to two years.
section_path: I. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 116 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the infliction of beatings or other violent actions causing physical pain but not resulting in the consequences specified in Article 115 of the Criminal Code shall be punishable by a fine of up to RUB 40,000, or by the seizure of the convicted person's wages or other income for a period of up to three months, or by community service for a period of up to 360 hours, or by corrective labour for a period of up to six months or by imprisonment for a term of up to three months.
section_path: I. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 116 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the same acts as in Article 116 § 1, if committed for disorderly motives or on grounds of political, ideological, racial, national or religious hatred or enmity or on grounds of hostility or hatred towards any social group, shall be punishable by community service for a period of up to 360 hours, or by corrective labour for a period of up to one year, or by restriction of liberty for a period of up to two years, or by compulsory labour for a period of up to two years, or by imprisonment for a term of up to six months or by deprivation of liberty for a period of up to two years.
section_path: I. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 282 § 1 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that actions aimed at inciting hatred or enmity and humiliating the dignity of an individual or a group of individuals on the grounds of gender, race, ethnic origin, language, background, religious beliefs or membership of a social group, committed publicly or in the mass media, shall be punishable by a fine of from RUB 100,000 to RUB 300,000 or an amount equivalent to the convicted person's wages or other income for a period of from one to two years, or by the withdrawal of the right to hold certain posts or carry out certain activities for a period of up to three years, or by community service for a period of up to 360 hours, or by corrective labour for a period of up to one year, or by compulsory labour for a period of up to two years or by deprivation of liberty of up to two years.
section_path: I. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 282 § 2 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation provides that the same actions as in Article 282 § 1, if committed with the use of violence or the threat of its use, by a person using his or her official position, or by an organised group, are punishable by a fine of RUB 100,000 to RUB 500,000 or an amount equivalent to the convicted person's wages or other income for a period of from one to three years, or by the withdrawal of the right to hold certain posts or carry out certain activities for a period of up to five years, or by community service for a period of up to 480 hours, or by corrective labour for a period of from one to two years, or by compulsory labour for a period of up to five years or by deprivation of liberty of up to five years.
section_path: I. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Until 3 July 2016 any form of 'battery' had constituted a criminal offence under Article 116 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.
section_path: I. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: On 3 July 2016 the 'non-aggravated' form of battery was decriminalised and reclassified as an administrative offence under Article 6.1.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation.
section_path: I. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE

text: Article 6.1.1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of the Russian Federation provides that the infliction of beatings or the commission of other violent actions that cause physical pain but do not result in the consequences specified in Article 115 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation shall, as long as these acts do not constitute a criminal offense, entail the imposition of an administrative fine of from RUB 5,000 to RUB 30,000, or administrative detention for a period of from ten to fifteen days or community service for a period of from sixty to 120 hours.

text: In accordance with the Constitutional Court of the Russian Federation's ruling of 23 September 2014 on the constitutionality of Article 6.21 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences of Russia, the concept of 'a social group' may apply to a group of people on the basis of their sexual orientation.
section_path: I. RELEVANT DOMESTIC LAW AND PRACTICE
C. Case-law of the Constitutional Court

text: On 31 March 2010 the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe adopted Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 to member States on measures to combat discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe provides that member states should ensure effective, prompt and impartial investigations into alleged cases of crimes and other incidents where the sexual orientation or gender identity of the victim is reasonably suspected to have constituted a motive for the perpetrator.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe provides that member states should ensure that particular attention is paid to the investigation of crimes and incidents allegedly committed by law enforcement officials or by other persons acting in an official capacity, and that those responsible are effectively brought to justice and, where appropriate, punished in order to avoid impunity.

Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 of the Committee of Ministers of the Council of Europe provides that member states should ensure that when determining sanctions, a bias motive related to sexual orientation or gender identity may be taken into account as an aggravating circumstance.

In its report on the Russian Federation adopted on 4 December 2018 (CRI(2019)2), the European Commission against Racism and Intolerance noted that sexual orientation and gender identity are not explicitly enumerated as prohibited grounds in the relevant provisions of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation, such as Articles 282, 136 and 63.

The European Commission against Racism and Intolerance noted in its report CRI(2019)2 that Articles 282, 136 and 63 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation include a reference to 'any social group' in their list of grounds, and that the Constitutional Court of the Russian Federation in 2014 found that this term can apply to a group of individuals with a specific sexual orientation.

The European Commission against Racism and Intolerance noted in its report CRI(2019)2 that the Constitutional Court of the Russian Federation's 2014 interpretation that 'any social group' can apply to a group of individuals with a specific sexual orientation does not seem to be reflected in regular court practice.

The European Commission against Racism and Intolerance noted in its report CRI(2019)2 that the United Nations expressed concern about the fact that Article 63 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation on aggravating circumstances does not appear to have ever been applied to cases involving violence against LGBTI persons, in spite of a high number of such incidents.

The European Commission against Racism and Intolerance noted in its report CRI(2019)2 that the Russian authorities informed the European Commission against Racism and Intolerance that they do not see a need to name sexual orientation and gender identity expressly in the list of grounds of Articles 282, 136 and 63 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.

In its report CRI(2019)2, the European Commission against Racism and Intolerance recommended that the Russian authorities amend all existing legislation in order to include explicitly the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity in the list of protected grounds, in particular in Articles 282, 136 and 63 of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation.

In its concluding observations on the seventh periodic report of the Russian Federation of 28 April 2015 (CCPR/C/RUS/7), the United Nations Human Rights Committee expressed concern that Article 63 § 1 (e) of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation, recognising as aggravated circumstances the commission of an offence for reasons of 'hatred or enmity' or 'hate or hostility towards a given social group', does not appear to have ever been applied to cases involving violence against LGBTI individuals.

In its concluding observations CCPR/C/RUS/7, the United Nations Human Rights Committee stated that the Russian Federation should clearly and officially state that it does not tolerate any form of social stigmatization of homosexuality, bisexuality or transsexuality, or hate speech, discrimination or violence against persons based on their sexual orientation or gender identity.

In its concluding observations CCPR/C/RUS/7, the United Nations Human Rights Committee stated that the Russian Federation should take all the steps necessary to ensure the investigation, prosecution and punishment of any act of violence motivated by the victim's sexual orientation or gender identity and apply the provisions of Article 63 § 1 (e) of the Criminal Code of the Russian Federation to such acts.
